results.title: Power Analysis for Parameter Estimation in Structural Equation Modeling: A Discussion and Tutorial
results.content: In this article, we (a) distinguish power to detect model misspecification from power to detect a target effect, (b) report the results of a simulation study on power to detect a target regression coefficient in a three-predictor latent regression model, and (c) introduce a user-friendly Shiny app, pwrSEM, for conducting power analysis for detecting target effects in structural equation models. [![: Simulation results: power as a function of the total sample size (N), for all combinations of population effect size (β YX ; columns), factor loadings (λ; rows), number of indicators per latent factor (p/f ), and analysis model (structural equation model [SEM] or compositescore regression).]()]( "Fig. 3. [Simulation results: power as a function of the total sample size (N), for all combinations of population effect size (β YX ; columns), factor loadings (λ; rows), number of indicators per latent factor (p/f ), and analysis model (structural equation model [SEM] or compositescore regression). We considered several pieces of information when making our assessment, including the results of simulation studies using factor analysis (e.g., Mundfrom et al., 2005;Wolf et al., 2013), the samples sizes used in previous validation work with the SCOPE in nonsport populations (Gaudreau et al., 2022;Tape et al., 2024), and the results of a power analysis using the pwrSEM shiny app (with inputted parameters based on the results from Gaudreau et al., 2022;Wang & Rhemtulla, 2021). Conducting a power analysis can be challenging for researchers who plan to analyze their data using structural equation models (SEMs), particularly when Monte Carlo methods are used to obtain power. In this paper we (a) distinguish power to detect model misspecification from power to detect a target effect, (b) report the results of a simulation study on power to detect a target regression coefficient in a 3-predictor latent regression model, and (c) introduce a Shiny app, pwrSEM, for user-friendly power analysis for detecting target effects in structural equation models. results.title: Penalized Models for Analysis of Multiple Mediators - PMC
results.content: We extend the use of structural equation models for analysis of multiple mediators by creating a sparse group lasso penalized model such that the penalty considers the natural groupings of parameters that determine mediation, as well as encourages sparseness of the model parameters. Alternatively, structural equation models (SEMs) are preferred for multiple mediators because they can be used to simultaneously estimate the parameters representing direct and indirect effects, they provide explicit ways to model the relationships among the variables, and they account for the correlations among the mediators (Hoyle, 2012; Preacher & Hayes, 2008; T. (Jacobucci et al., 2016) used either an L1 penalty (e.g., ) or L2 penalty (e.g., ) on all parameters, for general penalized SEMs. In contrast, we propose a different type of penalty, based on sparse group lasso that is tailored for mediation analyses. Although our models are conceptually similar to regularization of general SEMs (Jacobucci et al., 2016), our sparse group lasso penalty for mediation groupings, the details of our iterative algorithm, and our computational efficiencies make *regmed* unique. Furthermore, by capitalizing on the special structure of the implied covariance matrix imposed by our mediation model, we were able to tailor our software to be much more computationally efficient than the generic *regsem* R software for penalized SEMs (Jacobucci et al., 2016). Finally, our approach provides a way to directly evaluate whether a biomarker directly mediates the effect of exposure on an outcome, in contrast to penalized models that assume latent factors as mediators (Derkach et al., 2019). By simulations, we found that our approach can have a higher chance of false inference of mediators when non-mediators have very strong effects, the mediators are highly correlated, sample size is small (relative to the number of mediators), and more emphasis is placed on grouping mediators than encouraging sparse models. In the study of childhood trauma and reactive cortisol stress with 85 subjects, we started with 40 potential mediators in the penalized model, which means 80 parameters for the and , a large number of parameters.

results.title: Power and Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Trials with Patient-Reported Outcomes under Equal and Unequal Group Sizes Based on Graded Response Model: A Simulation Study
results.content: Power and Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Trials with Patient-Reported Outcomes under Equal and Unequal Group Sizes Based on Graded Response Model: A Simulation Study - Value in Health. To provide a valid sample size strategy based on simulation and to evaluate the statistical power in clinical trials with patient-reported outcomes (PROs) based on a polytomous item response theory model—the graded response model (GRM)—and to compare this framework with the classical test theory (CTT) approach. Powers computed from GRM-based approach (1 – _β_ GRM) and the expected power obtained by the classical formula (1 – _β_ C) for the Wald test comparing the mean values of the latent trait in the two arms of an RCT for different values of the group effects, items, and category of the questionnaire (_α_ = 5%) with equal sample sizes per group (_r_ = 1). Powers computed from GRM-based approach (1 – _β_ GRM) and the expected power obtained by the classical formula (1 – _β_ C) for the Wald test comparing the mean values of the latent trait in the two arms of an RCT for different values of the group effects, items, and category of the questionnaire (_α_ = 5%) with unequal sample sizes per group (_r_ = 2). Powers computed from GRM-based approach (1 – _β_ GRM) and the expected power obtained by the classical formula (1 – _β_ C) for the Wald test comparing the mean values of the latent trait in the two arms of an RCT for different values of the group effects, items, and category of the questionnaire (_α_ = 5%) with unequal sample sizes per group (_r_ = 3). In particular, the effect of a nonsymmetrical score, which is prevalent in PRO measures, or the effect of precision of the main study parameters (item parameters, variance of latent trait, and group effects) on the obtained power can be evaluated during the analysis of the RCTs. The results of this study show that the impact of the most influential factors—the number of patients required in each arm of an RCT, the group allocation ratio, group effects, and the number of categories—on power and sample size calculations of GRM-based and CTT-based approaches was similar.

results.title: [2309.00866] Tutorial: a priori estimation of sample size, effect size, and statistical power for cluster analysis, latent class analysis, and multivariate mixture models
results.content: # Title:Tutorial: a priori estimation of sample size, effect size, and statistical power for cluster analysis, latent class analysis, and multivariate mixture models. View a PDF of the paper titled Tutorial: a priori estimation of sample size, effect size, and statistical power for cluster analysis, latent class analysis, and multivariate mixture models, by Edwin S Dalmaijer. For traditional statistical tests, one would typically determine an acceptable level of statistical power, (gu)estimate effect size, and then use both values to compute the required sample size. The table shows the minimum numbers of observations per expected subgroup (sample size) and features (measured variables) to achieve acceptable statistical power, and can be readily used in study design.
